facts.text: The object is a pectoral in the form of a double-headed serpent, made of cedro wood (Cedrela odorata) and covered with a mosaic of turquoise and red thorny oyster shell (Spondylus princeps).
It is carved from a single piece of Spanish cedarwood.
The front and both heads are covered with turquoise mosaic.
The hollowed-out back of the body was originally gilded.
The back, once gilded, is now plain.
The back was hollowed out, possibly to make the sculpture lighter.
Only the heads are decorated on both sides.
The teeth in the two open mouths are made from conch shell (Strombus).
Two resins were used as adhesive: pine resin and Bursera resin (copal).
In the mouths the resin is coloured red with hematite.
The worked tiles were carefully selected and graded by size and colour, then laid in to recreate the subtle patterning of the snake's scales.
The turquoise was cut and ground using stone tools.
The heads may originally have had inlaid eyes of pyrite or obsidian.
Flickering tongues might have been attached to the holes in the centre of the lower jaws.
Beeswax adhesive survives around the eye sockets.
The museum gives the production date as 1400-1521.
It measures 20.30 centimetres high, 43.30 centimetres wide and 5.90 centimetres deep.
The two holes at the top indicate that it may have been worn on the chest as a pectoral.
This maquizcoatl might have been an insignia worn or held by an effigy of Huitzilopochtli or by one of his impersonators.
The double-headed serpent may represent a 'sky-band', symbolizing the celestial realm.
It was an emblem of authority.
It is not known how the sculpture left Mexico.
It is considered possible that it was among the goods obtained by the conquistador Hernán Cortés.
The museum registered the serpent as purchased in September 1894.
It is on display in Room 27 (Mexico), Display Case 6, at the British Museum.
Turquoise was highly valued in Mesoamerica.
Aztec trading emissaries (pochteca) obtained turquoise from mines in what is now the southwest United States, far beyond the limits of the Aztec empire.
The Nahuatl term 'coatl' can be translated as both serpent and twin.
Double-headed serpents (maquizcoatl) were considered to be the bearers of bad omens and were associated with elite figures.
The Mexica believed that anyone finding a double-headed serpent in their path should place it on their arm; if the serpent could not be moved it meant that death was approaching.
The intense blue-green hues of turquoise evoke associations with Quetzalcoatl ('feathered serpent'), one of the most powerful Aztec deities and culture heroes.
The sculpture is one of nine Mexican turquoise mosaics in the British Museum.

text: Script ready: "Flash, Flip, Knock", 2 scene(s), NEEDS_HUMAN.
The script did not fully pass its own review (NEEDS_HUMAN); filming it anyway.

shots.narration: Whoa! I'm a serpent with two heads. I'm carved from one piece of cedarwood. Maybe I was worn on the chest.
shots.action: A white flash pops; both sockets fill with round blinking eyes; the two heads jerk round to stare at the lens. Then It peels off the black, sags, wriggles free, both heads shaking off dust, grinning. Then It whips over fast in mid-air like a flipped pancake, showing its plain hollow cedar back; one head slams down on the wood, TOCK, the body shuddering, tiles rattling. Then It flips back face-front, drops hard into its photo pose; both heads tilt up, eyes darting to the two small top holes; it freezes, blinking.

shots.narration: I might have been worn by Huitzilopochtli's effigy. I was an emblem of authority. Now I'm on display in Room twenty-seven.
shots.action: One eye on each head blinks; both heads swing slowly down to the lens. Then The serpent rises, both chins lifting. Then The serpent surges across the hall, whips round a pillar, bursts through smoke and snaps rigid, hanging chest-high, the brazier flame leaping. Then It darts in and coils hard into its S-curves; firelight gutters to black; one light ripple runs head to head and fades.
